subject: korean
title: Why was Jisu late?
goal: Choose the explanation that fits all the clues in a short chat about a past event, and say which clue carries most weight and what is still uncertain.
thinking: Inferring an unstated reason from several clues
Testing each explanation against every clue
Saying what the clues cannot prove
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks what the speaker says happened. Here nobody states the reason; you must build it from scattered clues and say how sure you can be.
prerequisites: Reads short chat messages in the past tense (-았/었어요)
material:
A study group chat (스터디 단체 대화방) the day after a meeting. Jisu arrived late and nobody asked her directly why.
민호: 어제 스터디에 지수 씨가 40분 늦게 왔어요.
하나: 맞아요. 처음에는 전화를 해도 안 받았어요.
민호: 도착했을 때 신발이 다 젖어 있었어요.
지수: 휴대폰이 꺼져서 연락을 못 했어요. 정말 죄송해요.

steps.prompt: Which explanation of Jisu's lateness fits ALL four clues (late, no answer to calls, wet shoes, phone off)?

options.text: She overslept, then hurried to the café without checking her phone.
options.reveals: This explains being late, but nothing in it explains the wet shoes. Check each explanation against every clue.

options.text: She forgot about the meeting until a friend called to ask where she was.
options.reveals: If her phone was off, nobody could have reached her by call, and she is apologizing for lateness, not for forgetting.

options.text: Something soaked her shoes on the way, and then her phone went off.
options.reveals: This one accounts for the delay, the wet shoes and the missed calls at the same time, without choosing a specific cause that the chat does not give.

options.text: She did not want to come, so she arrived late on purpose and ignored calls.
options.reveals: The text shows an apology (정말 죄송해요) and a practical problem (phone off). Nothing points to a wish to avoid the meeting.

steps.explain: Wet shoes plus a phone that went off point to one event on the way (weather or an accident) that explains several clues at once. Rain is a likely cause but not proven: a puddle or a spilled drink would also fit.
hints: List the four clues, then test each explanation against all of them, not only the first one.
Prefer the explanation that covers the most clues without adding new facts.

steps.prompt: In English, name the TWO clues that support your choice most, quoting the Korean for each, and name one other thing that could also have happened.

checks.label: quotes at least two separate Korean phrases
gives a reason (because / shows / suggests / fits / means ...)
admits an uncertainty or another possibility
patterns: \b(could|might|may|maybe|perhaps|possibly|probably|not sure|unless|another|other explanation|alternatively|not certain|cannot be sure|can't be sure|not proven|unsure|else|alternative\w*|possib\w*)\b

selfAssess: Do my two clues come from the chat itself, not from my imagination?
Is the 'other possibility' really different from my main explanation?
Did I say why a clue matters, not only copy it?

modelAnswers.text: '신발이 다 젖어 있었어요' shows she was outside in wet weather, and '휴대폰이 꺼져서' explains why she could not answer calls. Together they suggest rain and a dead phone, but she might also have fallen into a puddle, so it is not certain.
Two clues: '전화를 해도 안 받았어요' and '신발이 다 젖어 있었어요'. They suggest she was on the road without a working phone. Maybe the phone battery died, or the phone got wet; I cannot be sure which.
modelAnswers.note: Different clue pair and a different alternative; both are valid.

modelAnswers.text: Wet shoes (신발이 다 젖어 있었어요) and phone off (휴대폰이 꺼져서) fit a story of getting soaked on the way. She may have fallen in a puddle instead of being caught in rain.

badAnswers.text: It was the rain, because it rained.
badAnswers.why: No Korean clue quoted, no uncertainty, and the rain is asserted, not inferred.
Only copies Korean; gives no reasoning and no other possibility.

badAnswers.text: I think rain 신발 because shoes. might
badAnswers.why: Only one Korean word, no second clue, and no real reasoning.

badAnswers.text: 신발이 다 젖어 있었어요. It might have rained.
badAnswers.why: Quotes only one clue and gives no reason.

steps.humanReview: Whether the two quoted clues really support the explanation, and whether the alternative is a genuine one.
hints: Quote exactly the words that carry the clue.
Ask yourself: what else could make shoes wet or a phone go off?

rubric.full: Quotes two clues from the chat and explains what each shows
rubric.partial: Quotes clues but does not say what they show
rubric.none: Gives a conclusion with no clue

rubric.full: Names a different possibility and says what it would change

alternatives: The explanation 'she fell into a puddle / spilled a drink' also explains the shoes; accept it if the student connects it to the phone.
Citing 정말 죄송해요 as a clue is acceptable if the student explains that it shows she was at fault for the delay.
hardCases: Some students choose option a and justify it with the apology; the wet shoes remain unexplained, so ask them to test the other clues.

cautions.language: Past-tense chat style (-았/었어요, -아서/어서) and a 'phone off' sentence are everyday Korean; the English answer lets learners reason without needing advanced Korean writing.
cautions.culture: Study groups at cafés are common; people often apologize at length for lateness. Rain is assumed only as one possibility.
cautions.accessibility: Text only, no images. Each speaker label is followed by a colon so a screen reader announces who is speaking.

auto: The choice against the key
Presence of a Korean quote, a reason word and a hedge in the English answer
human: Whether the clues are used correctly and the alternative is real

subject: korean
title: Hana's weekend does not add up
goal: Find the two lines of a short conversation that cannot both be true, then repair the account in natural past-tense Korean.
thinking: Comparing statements for contradiction
Locating which details conflict (time of day, place)
Repairing an account with a minimal change
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to read a dialogue for facts. Here the dialogue contains a conflict, and you must find it and repair it.
prerequisites: Reads past-tense sentences (-았/었어요) and time words (하루 종일, 저녁)
material: On Monday morning, a coworker asks Hana about her weekend.

steps.prompt: Two of Hana's lines cannot both be true. Click ONE of them (either one counts).
lines: 가: 하나 씨, 주말에 뭐 했어요?
나: 토요일에는 감기에 걸려서 하루 종일 집에서 쉬었어요.
나: 일요일에는 친구들하고 같이 점심을 먹었어요.
나: 토요일 저녁에는 친구 결혼식에 가서 사진을 많이 찍었어요.
steps.explain: Lines 2 and 4 conflict: 'all day at home' (하루 종일 집에서) cannot be true if she was at a wedding on Saturday evening. Line 3 is about Sunday, so it is not part of the conflict.
hints: Underline the day and the time of day in every line.
Compare what each Saturday line says about where Hana was.

steps.prompt: Rewrite ONE of the two conflicting lines in Korean (past tense, polite style) so that Hana's Saturday makes sense.

checks.label: is a changed line, not a copy of one of the original lines
does not keep both 'all day at home' and an attended wedding
shows how the two parts fit (another part of the day, not going, no wedding, or sick but still went)

selfAssess: Can both of my Saturday lines now be true at the same time?
Did I change as little as possible?
Is my sentence natural Korean (particles, past ending)?

modelAnswers.text: 토요일 아침에는 집에서 쉬었고, 저녁에는 친구 결혼식에 가서 사진을 많이 찍었어요.
토요일 저녁에도 집에서 책을 읽고 쉬었어요.
modelAnswers.note: Changes the second line instead; also valid.

modelAnswers.text: 토요일에는 감기에 걸렸지만 약을 먹고 저녁에 친구 결혼식에 갔어요.
modelAnswers.note: Repairs line 2: sick, but better by the evening.

modelAnswers.text: 토요일 저녁에는 감기 때문에 친구 결혼식에 못 갔어요.
modelAnswers.note: Repairs line 4: she did not go.

badAnswers.text: 토요일에는 하루 종일 쉬었고 저녁에 결혼식에 갔어요.
badAnswers.why: Keeps the conflict: 'all day' and the evening wedding.
Present tense, and says nothing about the repaired time.

badAnswers.text: 토요일에는 감기에 걸려서 하루 종일 집에서 쉬었어요.
badAnswers.why: A copy of the original line, nothing is repaired.

badAnswers.text: 토요일 저녁에는 친구 결혼식에 가서 사진을 많이 찍었어요.
badAnswers.why: A copy of the original line, nothing is repaired.

steps.humanReview: Naturalness of the Korean and whether the repaired line really removes the conflict.
hints: Decide which of the two lines you will change, then ask what exactly makes the two lines clash.
Change the time or the activity so that both Saturday lines can be true on the same day.

rubric.full: Selects a line from the conflicting pair and sees why it clashes
rubric.partial: Selects a Saturday line without seeing the clash

rubric.full: Rewritten line is consistent with the other Saturday line and in natural past tense

alternatives: Changing line 3 (Sunday) is not a repair; the conflict is in the Saturday lines.
A student may split the day: 오전에는 쉬었고 저녁에는 ... ; this is a good repair.
hardCases: A sentence such as '일요일 저녁에는 결혼식에 갔어요' passes no conflict but trips the surface check 'all day + wedding' if 하루 종일 is kept elsewhere; the self-assessment decides.

cautions.language: 하루 종일 means 'the whole day'; the particle -에는 marks contrast between days.
cautions.culture: A wedding on a Saturday evening is common in Korea. 감기 (a cold) is a neutral reason for resting.
cautions.accessibility: Dialogue is split into labeled lines read in order; no tables or images.

auto: Which line is clicked
Past tense, 'Saturday' and absence of both conflicting details
human: Naturalness and consistency of the rewritten sentence

subject: korean
topic: plan messages: asking what you need
title: Which question do I need to ask?
goal: Decide which missing pieces of information you need before you can accept an invitation, then ask for exactly those in polite Korean.
thinking: Matching missing information to your own constraints
Ignoring interesting but irrelevant details
Forming a clear question about a future plan
differsFromPlain: Plain practice answers questions about a message. Here the message is incomplete and you decide which questions would settle the answer.
prerequisites: Can ask polite questions with 몇 시, 언제
material:
Your classmate Hana sends this message on Wednesday. On Saturdays you work until 1:00 p.m., and you can spend at most 10,000 won on the activity.
하나: 이번 토요일에 서울숲에서 자전거를 탈 거예요. 자전거는 한 시간에 5,000원이에요. 같이 갈래요?

steps.prompt: Which TWO things must you find out before you can say yes or no?

options.text: Which brand of bike they will rent
options.reveals: The brand changes neither your work hours nor your budget, so the answer will not depend on it.

options.text: What time they will start riding
options.reveals: Your Saturday work ends at 1:00, so the start time decides whether the day is even possible.

options.text: Who else is coming
options.reveals: Friends can matter to you, but neither of your two limits depends on it.

options.text: Where in the park they will meet
options.reveals: You will need it later, but you can still accept or refuse without it.

options.text: How many hours they plan to ride
options.reveals: At 5,000 won an hour, the number of hours decides whether you stay within 10,000 won.

steps.explain: Your two limits are a work end time (1:00) and a budget (10,000 won). The start time answers the first limit and the number of hours (times 5,000 won) answers the second.
hints: Write down your two limits first, then ask which missing detail would let you test each one.
For each option, ask: if I knew this, would my yes/no change?

steps.prompt: Write your reply to Hana in Korean (polite style): ask her the questions you chose, without saying yes or no yet.

checks.label: asks how long or until when
does not say yes or no yet
patterns: 같이 갈게요|갈 수 있어요|갈 수 없어요|못 가요|안 갈게요

selfAssess: Does my message let Hana answer both questions in one reply?
Is it clear that I have not decided yet?
Did I keep the polite ending?

modelAnswers.text: 토요일 몇 시에 시작할 거예요? 그리고 몇 시간 정도 탈 거예요?
저는 토요일 1시까지 일해요. 자전거는 몇 시에 탈 거예요? 언제까지 탈 거예요?
modelAnswers.note: Gives a reason for asking and uses 언제까지 for duration.

modelAnswers.text: 몇 시부터 몇 시까지 탈 거예요?
modelAnswers.note: Start and end in one question.

badAnswers.why: Says yes without asking anything.
Asks an irrelevant question.

badAnswers.text: 좋아요! 몇 시에 시작해요? 몇 시간 타요?
badAnswers.why: Says yes before the two limits are checked.

badAnswers.text: 저는 토요일 1시까지 일해요. 몇 시에 시작해요?
badAnswers.why: Asks only about the start; the length (the budget) is missing.

steps.humanReview: Politeness level and whether the questions are clear.
hints: Each question should match one of your two limits.
Use -(으)ㄹ 거예요? for the plan, and 몇 시 / 몇 시간 for the amounts.

rubric.full: Chooses both decisive details and gives up the others
rubric.none: Chooses only interesting but irrelevant details

rubric.full: Message asks both decisive questions politely
rubric.none: Asks nothing relevant or just accepts

alternatives: Asking where to meet as well is reasonable; it is not required to decide.
Asking about price again is not needed since Hana already stated it.
hardCases: If Hana's plan starts at 2:00 and lasts three hours, you could still go if you cut it to two hours: the decision may involve negotiating, not only yes/no.

cautions.language: The question words 몇 시 (what time) and 몇 시간 (how many hours) are easy to confuse; the checks separate them.
cautions.culture: Renting bikes in a city park is a common outing; prices are made up. 원 is the Korean won.
cautions.accessibility: Message is plain text; the time and money are written with digits.

auto: The two chosen options
Polite ending and presence of both question types
human: Clarity and naturalness of the questions

subject: korean
title: A Saturday that fits the schedule
goal: Find several different plans that satisfy all the time rules in a friend's message, then tell the friend your plan in Korean.
thinking: Reading several conditions at once
Finding more than one plan that satisfies them all
Checking a plan against every rule
differsFromPlain: Plain practice reads a schedule. Here you build several valid schedules from the rules and discover which options are impossible.
prerequisites: Reads clock times in Korean (오전, 오후, 낮 12시) and digits + 시
material:
친구의 문자 (a friend's text message):
토요일 계획이에요.
- 오전 11시에 만나요.
- 점심은 늦어도 오후 1시에는 먹기 시작할 거예요. 점심은 1시간 걸려요.
- 점심을 다 먹은 뒤에 영화를 볼 거예요. 영화는 2시간이에요. 낮 12시, 오후 2시, 오후 4시에만 시작해요.
- 영화가 끝나면 바로 집에 갈 거예요. 극장에서 집까지 1시간 걸리고, 저녁 6시까지 집에 와야 해요.

steps.prompt: Write three different plans that satisfy every rule. Use the 24-hour number for the start time (낮 12시 = 12, 오후 2시 = 14, 오후 4시 = 16). Lunch starts at l; the movie starts at m.

constraints.ok: Lunch starts on a whole hour between 11 and 13.
constraints.fail: Lunch must start after the 11:00 meeting and no later than 13:00, on a whole hour.

constraints.ok: The movie starts at a time that is shown.
The movie starts after lunch is over.
constraints.fail: Lunch takes 1 hour and must be finished before the movie starts.
The movie lasts 2 hours and the trip home 1 hour; you must be home by 18:00.

steps.explain: One rule removes the 4 p.m. movie (it would end at 18:00 and leave no time to travel), and another rule requires lunch to be over before the movie. Four plans remain.
hints: Check one rule at a time; start by finding which movie times can ever work.
Choose a movie time first, then ask which lunch start times fit before it.

steps.prompt: Send your plan to your friend in Korean (polite style): say when you will eat lunch and when you will see the movie.
selfAssess: Does my message match one of the plans that passed the rules?
Are both times clear to my friend?
Did I use the plan/future ending?

modelAnswers.text: 11시에 만나서 점심을 먹고 2시에 영화를 볼 거예요.
저는 12시에 점심을 먹기 시작하고 2시에 영화를 볼 거예요.

badAnswers.why: No clock times, so the friend cannot check the plan.
Does not mention lunch, the movie, or the plan.

steps.humanReview: Whether the times written in Korean match the plan the student built.
hints: Use a plan you built in the previous step.
Put the time before 에, and the activity before 을/를.

rubric.full: Three different plans, all satisfying every rule
Message states both times, matches a valid plan, uses a plan ending

alternatives: Only four distinct plans exist, so any three are correct.
Writing the time as 오후 2시 instead of 14시 in the message is fine.
hardCases: A student who keeps the 4 p.m. movie has misread the last rule; the build feedback shows which rule fails.

cautions.language: Korean clock times use native numbers for hours (한 시, 두 시 ...) in speech; digits are also accepted in writing.
cautions.culture: Movies and lunch on a Saturday are universal; times are invented.
cautions.accessibility: The 24-hour number is explained in the prompt; no schedule graphic is used.

auto: Each built plan against the four rules
Plan ending, mentions and times in the message
human: Whether the written plan matches a built plan and is natural

subject: korean
topic: revising an inference as a story unfolds
title: Sujin's trip
goal: Revise your guess about a cancelled trip as three parts of a conversation appear, then write a helpful offer.
thinking: Inferring a reason from small hints
Revising a guess when new information arrives
Using the inferred situation to choose a helpful reply
differsFromPlain: Plain practice reads a whole dialogue once. Here the dialogue appears in three parts and you must update your guess each time.
material: Minji and her friend Sujin are talking about a trip to Jeju next week.

steps.prompt: Read each part, choose the reading that seems most likely so far, then continue.
hints: Decide using only what has appeared so far.
Notice what comes after -는데 and -아서: it often hides the result.
steps.reflect: A first guess can be reasonable and still be replaced. Notice which new sentence made you change: the reason (발표) first, then the plan (대신 갈 사람).

stages.info: 수진: 다음 주 제주도 여행은 못 갈 것 같아요. 비행기표를 벌써 샀는데…
stages.ask: What is the most likely reason at this point?

options.text: She cannot afford the trip
options.reveals: She has already bought the ticket, so money does not look like the main problem.

options.text: Something outside her control has come up
options.reveals: The trailing 는데… signals regret about money already spent and a result she cannot change.

options.text: She no longer likes Jeju
options.reveals: '벌써 샀는데' shows she wanted to go; nothing says her wish has changed.

options.text: She bought the ticket for the wrong date
options.reveals: A possible reading of '샀는데…' as a mistake, though the sentence does not say it.

stages.after: Both an outside event and a ticket mistake fit the unfinished sentence. More information is needed.

stages.info:
민지: 무슨 일 있어요?
수진: 회사에서 다음 주에 갑자기 발표를 하게 됐어요. 준비를 해야 해서요.

options.text: She is sick
options.reveals: No illness is mentioned; the reason is work.

options.text: She made a mistake with the ticket date
options.reveals: Her explanation is about work, not the ticket.

options.text: A sudden work presentation
options.reveals: Her own reason (갑자기 발표를 하게 됐어요) states this.

options.text: She changed her mind
options.reveals: She gives a work reason; nothing suggests she changed her wish.

stages.after: Her reason is a presentation at work that she must prepare for. The ticket-mistake guess is gone.

stages.info:
민지: 표는 어떻게 해요? 취소하면 돈을 못 받는다고 했죠?
수진: 네. 그래서 대신 갈 수 있는 사람이 있는지 찾아보고 있어요.

options.text: Find someone to go in her place
options.reveals: She says she is looking for 대신 갈 수 있는 사람.

options.text: Cancel the ticket and get a refund
options.reveals: Minji notes that cancelling means no money back, and Sujin agrees.

options.text: Go anyway and prepare on the trip
options.reveals: She said she cannot go because she must prepare.

options.text: Move the trip to next month
options.reveals: Nothing in the conversation mentions changing the date.

stages.after: Because cancelling loses the money, her plan is to hand the trip to someone else.

steps.prompt: Minji wants to help. Write a short Korean message (polite style) that offers or suggests something about the ticket.

checks.label: is about the ticket or a replacement

selfAssess: Does my offer follow from what Sujin said (cannot cancel, needs a replacement)?
Did I offer something I can really do?
Is it kind as well as useful?

modelAnswers.text: 표를 취소하지 말고 제가 대신 갈 수 있는 친구를 찾아 볼게요.
수진 씨, 회사 일 때문에 힘들겠어요. 제 친구 중에 대신 갈 사람이 있는지 물어볼까요?
modelAnswers.note: Sympathy first, then an offer in question form.

badAnswers.why: Ignores that Sujin cannot go.
About the ticket but offers nothing.

steps.humanReview: Whether the offer fits the situation (no refund, replacement needed) and is natural.
hints: Use the last part of the conversation: what does Sujin need?
Use -(으)ㄹ게요 for an offer or -(으)ㄹ까요? for a suggestion.

rubric.full: Chooses a reasonable reading at every stage and sees why the earlier guess changed
rubric.none: Keeps one guess in spite of new information

rubric.full: Offer fits the inferred situation and is polite

alternatives: At stage 1 both 'something came up' and 'wrong date' are accepted.
Offering to find a replacement is only one good reply; sympathy plus a question is also fine.
hardCases: Suggesting a refund ignores Minji's own line that no refund is possible.

cautions.language: -는데… ends a sentence by leaving the result to the listener; this is the central grammar clue.
cautions.culture: Handing a plane ticket to a friend depends on airline rules; the story only assumes it is possible.
cautions.accessibility: Dialogue is revealed one part at a time, so a screen reader reads only the new part.

auto: The reasonable-set at each stage
Polite ending, ticket word and offer form

subject: korean
topic: revising a plan message for a new reader
title: Cancelling an appointment with a professor
goal: Decide what is missing from a cancellation message written for a friend, and rewrite it for a professor.
thinking: Evaluating a message for its reader
Adapting level of formality and content
Proposing a new plan
differsFromPlain: Plain practice changes a sentence ending. Here the same news must be rebuilt for a different reader: who you are, why, and what you propose.
material:
You had an office-hour appointment with your professor tomorrow at 3:00. Your class timetable has just changed and you cannot go. Your first draft:
"교수님, 내일 3시에 못 가요. 다른 일이 있어요. 다음에 갈게요."

steps.prompt: Which problems does this draft have for a PROFESSOR who reads it?

options.text: It does not say who is writing or which class
options.reveals: A professor receives many messages and needs to know the sender and the course.

options.text: It gives a time ('3시') that the professor will not recognize
options.reveals: The time and the word 내일 do show which appointment is meant; that part of the draft works.

options.text: It does not offer a new time
options.reveals: '다음에' is too vague for a professor to plan with.

options.text: It uses past tense for something in the future
options.reveals: The draft uses present/future forms (못 가요, 갈게요), not past.

options.text: It does not apologize for the change
options.reveals: A cancellation at short notice calls for an apology.

acceptable.reason: A reader may feel the apology is a matter of tone rather than content; sender and new time are still the essential gaps.

steps.explain: The draft names the appointment but not the writer, apologizes nowhere and leaves the next step open. Tense is fine and the time is clear.
hints: Imagine you are the professor: what would you still need to know after reading it?
Check each option against the actual words of the draft.

steps.prompt: Rewrite the message for the professor in Korean: introduce yourself and your class, apologize, give a short reason, and propose a new time. Use formal, polite endings.

checks.label: says who you are (class or 입니다)
proposes a new day or time

selfAssess: Could the professor reply 'yes' without any further question?
Is the new time specific (a day and a time of day)?
Do all my endings stay formal?

modelAnswers.text: 안녕하세요, 교수님. 한국어학개론 수업을 듣는 이지민입니다. 내일 3시 면담에 갈 수 없게 되어 죄송합니다. 수업 시간이 바뀌었습니다. 혹시 모레 오후 2시에 찾아뵈어도 될까요?
교수님, 안녕하세요. 수요일 3시 면담을 신청한 학생 김하나입니다. 갑자기 시간표가 바뀌어서 죄송합니다. 다음 주 월요일 오전은 어떠세요?
modelAnswers.note: Shorter; the proposal comes as a question.

badAnswers.text: 교수님, 내일 3시에 못 가요. 죄송해요. 다음에 갈게요.
badAnswers.why: No identification, no concrete new time, and not formal enough.
Introduces itself but has no apology and no new time.

steps.humanReview: Level of respect, naturalness and whether the new-time request is clear.
hints: Plan four parts: who I am, sorry, reason, new time.
Choose -ㅂ니다 or -세요 endings throughout.

rubric.full: Finds the three missing elements without false problems
Contains identity, apology, reason and concrete new time in formal Korean

alternatives: Some readers think a reason is optional; a short, general reason is acceptable.
Using 교수님 plus 께서 in a very formal rewrite is fine.
hardCases: A message with '미안합니다' is formal in ending but less suitable than 죄송합니다 to a professor; the check accepts both and self-assessment flags it.

cautions.language: Formal -ㅂ니다 style and 찾아뵙다 (humble 'to visit') are above everyday level; models show them but only formal endings are required.
cautions.culture: In Korean universities students address professors with 교수님 and formal speech; a message begins by identifying the course.
cautions.accessibility: Plain text; the draft is in quotation marks so it can be read apart from the instructions.

auto: The chosen problems
Formal ending, apology, identity and new-time words
human: Respectful tone and clarity of the proposal

subject: korean
title: A school trip notice with a time problem
goal: Find the clash in a trip notice, decide what can be concluded, and write a polite question that settles it.
thinking: Comparing times in a text
Deciding what cannot be concluded from the text alone
Asking a precise question
differsFromPlain: Plain practice reads the schedule. Here the schedule contradicts itself, and the right move is to ask rather than guess.
material: Your class received this notice from the teacher by message.

steps.prompt: Click ONE of the two lines whose times cannot both be right.
lines: [소풍 안내] 이번 토요일에 우리 반이 소풍을 갑니다.
아침 8시 30분까지 학교 앞에 모여서 9시에 버스를 탈 거예요.
버스를 타고 가면 공원에 11시 30분에 도착할 거예요.
공원에 도착한 뒤, 11시에 공원 앞 식당에서 점심을 먹을 거예요.
steps.explain: Lines 3 and 4 clash: the class arrives at the park at 11:30, but lunch 'after arriving' is at 11:00. Lines 1, 2 and 5 are consistent.
hints: Put the clock times of the lines in order and compare.
Check which event is said to come first, then check the times.

steps.prompt: What can you be sure of, and what should you do?

options.text: The text cannot show which time is wrong, so ask the teacher
options.reveals: Both lines could be the wrong one; asking is the only way to learn the true time.

options.text: The arrival time is the wrong one, so lunch really is at 11:00
options.reveals: Either time could be the typo; the text does not say which.

options.text: The lunch time is the wrong one, so lunch really is at 12:00
options.reveals: Nothing in the notice gives 12:00; this would add a fact.

options.text: Both are right: the class eats lunch before it arrives at the park
options.reveals: Line 4 says lunch is after arriving, so both cannot be right.

steps.explain: A clash shows that something is wrong, not what. Without more information, guessing 11:00 or 12:00 could make you late or early.
hints: Ask whether the text gives a way to decide between the two times.
Think about what happens if you guess wrong.

steps.prompt: Write a polite message to the teacher in Korean asking which time is correct.
selfAssess: Does my message point out which two details clash?
Could the teacher answer in one word or number?
Is it polite?

modelAnswers.text: 선생님, 공원에 11시 30분에 도착한다고 나와 있는데 점심은 11시예요. 어느 시간이 맞아요?
죄송하지만 확인하고 싶은 게 있어요. 점심 시간이 도착 시간보다 빨라요. 점심은 몇 시에 먹어요?
modelAnswers.note: Names the problem in plain words before asking.

badAnswers.why: Accepts the notice and asks nothing.
A question, but not about the clash.

steps.humanReview: Politeness and whether the question is specific enough to answer.
hints: Name the two details (도착, 점심) that you want to compare.
End with a question form: -나요? / -아/어요? / -(으)ㄹ까요?

rubric.full: Selects line 3 or 4 and understands that the pair clashes
rubric.partial: Selects a different line with a partial reason

rubric.full: Asks a precise polite question about the clash
rubric.none: Guesses a time or does not respond

alternatives: Either 'arrival 11:30' or 'lunch 11:00' could be the typo; do not accept a student who says which.
'어느 시간이 맞아요?' and '점심은 몇 시예요?' are both valid.
hardCases: Some students think the clash is between 8:30 and 9:00; those times are consistent ('by 8:30' gather, bus at 9:00).

cautions.language: 까지 (by/until) and 뒤에 (after) mark order; reading them carefully is the key.
cautions.culture: Class outings (소풍) with a packed lunch are a Korean school tradition; line 5 changes this one.
cautions.accessibility: Lines are numbered 1-5 when read; the notice has no images.

auto: The clicked line
The key choice
Polite ending, question form and mention of the details
human: Clarity and naturalness of the question

subject: korean
topic: conflicting accounts of a past event
title: Who was at the library?
goal: Weigh three accounts of the same afternoon and say what can and cannot be concluded, then name a way to find out more.
thinking: Comparing times in different accounts
Separating what is proved from what is merely consistent
Proposing a check
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks who said what. Here accounts conflict in a way that does not settle who is right, so you must reason about what is and is not shown.
material:
Class ends at 3:30. Minsu's home is a 30-minute walk from school, and he always walks (no bus). Three classmates talk the next day.
민수: 어제 수업이 끝나고 바로 집에 갔어요.
하나: 어제 4시쯤 도서관에서 민수 씨를 봤어요. 책을 빌리고 있었어요.
준호: 저는 4시 30분쯤 도서관에 있었는데 민수 씨는 못 봤어요.

steps.prompt: What can you conclude from the three accounts?

options.text: Hana's and Minsu's accounts clash, and Junho's does not decide between them
options.reveals: Minsu would not be home before 4:00 if he walked straight home, so he cannot also be at the library at 4:00; Junho's time is different.

options.text: Minsu is lying about going straight home, because Hana saw him at the library
options.reveals: One account conflicts with another, but a conflict does not show who is wrong or whether anyone lied.

options.text: Hana must be wrong, because Junho was at the library later and did not see Minsu
options.reveals: Junho arrived half an hour later than the time Hana gives, so his account says nothing about 4:00.

options.text: All three accounts can be true at the same time, since nobody gives a clock time
options.reveals: Home by 4:00 and borrowing a book in the library at 4:00 cannot both be true for one person.

steps.explain: Walking straight home takes until about 4:00, so Minsu cannot be at the library at 4:00. Either Minsu or Hana is wrong (or 'shortly after 4' is loosely meant). Junho arrived at 4:30, so he shows nothing about 4:00.
hints: Work out when Minsu would be home if he left at once.
Compare each account's time with the others: does any pair cover the same moment?

steps.prompt: In English, name one thing you would ask or check to find out who is right, quoting the Korean words that make you suspect it.

checks.label: proposes a way to check or ask

selfAssess: Would the check I proposed really separate the possibilities?
Did I quote the Korean words that matter?
Is my check practical?

modelAnswers.text: Ask Hana how sure she is about '4시쯤' and whether she spoke to him, and ask Minsu what time he got home, since '바로 집에 갔어요' should mean he was home about 4:00.
Check the library's loan record: if Minsu borrowed a book around '4시쯤' then Hana is right; Junho's '4시 30분쯤' is half an hour later, so it does not settle anything.
I would visit the library and look at the loan records to see when Minsu borrowed the book, because Hana says '4시쯤' but Minsu says '바로 집에 갔어요'.

badAnswers.why: No check and no Korean quoted.

badAnswers.text: I do not know who is right.
badAnswers.why: Does not use the evidence.

steps.humanReview: Whether the proposed check addresses the actual conflict.
hints: Pick the two times that clash and ask what could separate them.
A good check is something a person could really do.

rubric.full: Sees that the two accounts clash and that the third does not decide
rubric.partial: Sees the clash but wrongly uses the third
rubric.none: Sees no clash or declares one person a liar

rubric.full: A practical check that targets the conflicting times

alternatives: Asking friends or checking a record are both fine.
Saying 'Hana saw the wrong person' is acceptable as a hypothesis if the student proposes a check for it.
hardCases: Some students treat '바로' as loose; asking Minsu when he arrived home is a sensible check.

cautions.language: 쯤 (about), 바로 (immediately) and -고 (and then) shape the time logic; read them before judging.
cautions.culture: The scenario uses a short walk to school; Korean students often walk or take buses.
cautions.accessibility: Accounts are labeled by speaker and the timetable is stated in the material.

auto: The key choice
Quote, check-word and time reference in the English answer
human: Whether the check really separates the two accounts

subject: korean
topic: writing about the past so the reason can be inferred
title: Let the reader guess why
goal: Tell which short texts leave the reason unstated, then write your own so a reader can guess the reason without being told.
thinking: Distinguishing stated from implied reasons
Choosing details that carry a reason
Writing without the usual reason words
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to add a reason with -아서/어서. Here you do the opposite: use details so the reader infers the reason.
prerequisites: Knows past tense and -아서/어서/그래서 as reason words
Writes several simple sentences in Korean
material: Four short texts, each describing something that happened. In some, the reason is said in words; in others, the reader has to guess it.

steps.prompt: In which TWO texts is the reason NOT stated in words, but a reader can still guess it?

options.text: 어제 학교에 못 갔어요. 몸이 아파서 하루 종일 집에 있었어요.
options.reveals: '몸이 아파서' states the reason with -아서, so no guessing is needed.

options.text: 어제 아침에 병원에 갔어요. 약을 먹고 하루 종일 누웠어요.
options.reveals: No reason word appears, yet 병원, 약 and 누웠어요 together let the reader infer illness.

options.text: 어제 학교에 안 갔어요. 놀이공원에서 친구들하고 신나게 놀았어요.
options.reveals: Nothing is said about why she skipped school, but the activity makes a guess possible.

options.text: 어제 늦게 일어났어요. 그래서 학교에 늦었어요.
options.reveals: '그래서' states the cause and result directly.

steps.explain: In b and c the reader must connect details (hospital + medicine, or school day + amusement park). In a and d a reason word (-아서, 그래서) says it outright.
hints: Look for reason words such as -아서/어서, 그래서, -니까, 때문에.
Ask whether, with the reason words removed, you could still guess what happened.

steps.prompt: Write 2-3 Korean sentences about something that happened last week (yours or invented) so that the reason for one thing is not stated but can be guessed. Do not use -아서/어서/해서, 그래서, 때문에 or 이유.

checks.label: avoids direct reason words (-아서/어서/해서, 그래서, 때문에, 이유, -니까)

selfAssess: Could a classmate guess the reason from my details?
Did I avoid every direct reason word?
Is each sentence in natural past tense?

modelAnswers.text: 지난주 월요일에 아침 일찍 약국에 갔어요. 약을 사고 집에서 하루 종일 쉬었어요.
토요일에 새 운동화를 샀어요. 그리고 일요일 아침에 공원에서 달렸어요.
modelAnswers.note: The reason for buying shoes is left to the reader.

badAnswers.text: 어제 감기에 걸려서 학교에 못 갔어요.
badAnswers.why: States the reason with -아서.
Not past tense and only one sentence.

badAnswers.text: 어제 감기에 걸려서 학교에 못 갔어요. 집에서 쉬었어요.
badAnswers.why: States the reason with -려서.

badAnswers.text: 어제 몸이 아파서 학교에 못 갔어요. 집에서 쉬었어요.
badAnswers.why: States the reason with -파서.

steps.humanReview: Whether the reason can really be inferred and the Korean is natural.
hints: Pick the reason first, then choose two details that point to it without naming it.
Check for -아서, -어서, 그래서 before you finish.

rubric.full: Picks both implied-reason texts
Reason is clearly inferable and no direct reason word is used
rubric.partial: Reason is stated or too hidden

alternatives: Option c can be read as 'she wanted to play instead of attend'; accept that.
Texts about plans or feelings are fine if they are in past tense.
hardCases: A text where the hidden reason is not guessable by anyone else cannot be judged by the checks; a classmate or teacher should read it.

cautions.language: The ban on -아서/어서 excludes ordinary verbs such as '이어서'; the surface check may block rare innocent words.
cautions.culture: Visiting a pharmacy or hospital when ill is universal. 놀이공원 is a theme park.
cautions.accessibility: Choice texts are single sentences; the multi-select wording says 'TWO'.

auto: The two chosen texts
Past tense, two sentences and absence of direct reason words
human: Whether the reason can be inferred from the writer's details

subject: korean
title: A picnic in three messages
goal: Update your view of the group's plan as messages arrive, then write the final confirmation message.
thinking: Updating a plan when conditions change
Combining several people's limits
Writing a clear confirmation
differsFromPlain: Plain practice reads one chat message. Here the plan changes twice and you must combine different people's limits.
prerequisites: Understands days of the week and 오전/오후
material: Hana, Minsu and Jisu are planning a picnic by the Han River in their group chat.

steps.prompt: Read each message, choose the plan that fits so far, then continue.
hints: Use only the messages you have seen.
For each new message, ask which earlier detail it replaces.
steps.reflect: Each message removed one earlier detail and added a limit. Notice how the final plan needed Saturday (sandwiches), Sunday (picnic) and 5:30 (Jisu's limit) at the same time.

stages.info:
하나: 이번 토요일 2시에 한강에서 피크닉 어때요?
민수: 좋아요! 저는 샌드위치를 가져갈게요.
stages.ask: What is the plan so far?

options.text: Saturday 2:00 at the Han River; Minsu brings sandwiches
options.reveals: This matches both messages.

options.text: Saturday 2:00; Minsu buys sandwiches there
options.reveals: Minsu says 가져갈게요 (I'll bring), not buy there.

options.text: Sunday 2:00; Hana brings sandwiches
options.reveals: Hana proposed Saturday, and Minsu volunteered the sandwiches.

options.text: Saturday 3:00; Minsu brings sandwiches
options.reveals: The proposed time is 2:00.

stages.after: So far: Saturday, 2:00, Han River, sandwiches from Minsu.

stages.info:
지수: 토요일 오후에 비가 온대요.
하나: 그럼 일요일은 어때요? 일요일은 맑대요.
민수: 일요일은 오전에 일이 있어요. 오후 3시 이후에는 괜찮아요.
stages.ask: Which plan works for everyone now?

options.text: Saturday 2:00 anyway
options.reveals: Rain is forecast for Saturday afternoon.

options.text: Sunday 11:00
options.reveals: Minsu is busy on Sunday morning.

options.text: Sunday at 3:00 or later
options.reveals: Sunday is sunny and Minsu is free after 3:00.

stages.after: Sunday afternoon after 3:00 is the only slot named so far.

stages.info:
지수: 일요일 4시에 가는 건 좋은데, 그날 저녁 6시에 가족 모임이 있어서 5시 30분에는 가야 해요.
하나: 그럼 4시에 만나서 5시 반까지 놀아요. 민수 씨는 샌드위치 괜찮아요?
민수: 네, 토요일에 만들어서 가져갈게요.

options.text: Sunday 4:00-6:00; Minsu makes sandwiches Sunday morning
options.reveals: Jisu must leave at 5:30, and Minsu has something on Sunday morning.

options.text: Sunday 4:00-5:30; Minsu makes sandwiches on Saturday
options.reveals: Matches Hana's timing and Minsu's own plan.

options.text: Saturday 2:00 as first planned; Minsu brings sandwiches
options.reveals: Rain was forecast, so this plan was dropped.

options.text: Sunday 3:00-5:30; Minsu buys sandwiches there
options.reveals: Hana set 4:00, and Minsu says he will make them.

stages.after: Final plan: Sunday 4:00-5:30, Minsu makes the sandwiches on Saturday and brings them.

steps.prompt: Write the confirmation message to the group chat in Korean (polite style): the day, the time, when it ends, and who brings the sandwiches.

checks.label: says who brings the sandwiches (민수 + 샌드위치)

selfAssess: Is my message consistent with every limit in the chat?
Did I say who brings the food?
Would a person who reads only this message know what to do?

modelAnswers.text: 그럼 일요일 4시에 한강에서 만나요. 5시 반에는 끝낼 거예요. 샌드위치는 민수 씨가 가져오세요.
확정할게요! 일요일 오후 4시에 만나서 5시 30분까지 놀아요. 샌드위치는 민수 씨가 토요일에 만들어서 가져와요.

badAnswers.why: Wrong day and time; ignores the rain and Jisu's limit.
Missing times.
Does not say who brings the sandwiches.

steps.humanReview: Whether the message is clear and complete.
hints: Re-read the last stage for the day, start and end times.
Use -아/어요 or -(으)ㄹ게요 endings.

rubric.full: Reasonable choice at every stage and sees how earlier details were replaced
Contains day, start, end and who brings food in polite Korean

alternatives: Starting at 4:00 and ending around 5:30 is the only plan satisfying the stated limits; a student who adds a place is fine.
Writing 오후 4시 or 16시 is also acceptable.
hardCases: A student writes '4시 30분'; check that it is not the end time confused with start.

cautions.language: -대요 (they say) reports someone else's information; the chat uses it for the forecast.
cautions.culture: Han River picnics are popular; ordering delivery chicken is usual but sandwiches are the example here.
cautions.accessibility: Three speakers are labeled; the final plan is repeated in text.

auto: The reasonable-set at each stage
Day, times and polite ending in the final message
human: Whether the confirmation is clear and consistent
